constellations.name: Ursa Major
constellations.story: Long ago a kind queen named Callisto was turned into a bear by a jealous goddess. To keep her safe, the great god Zeus lifted her into the sky by her tail. That is why the bear's tail is so long! Her seven brightest stars make the Big Dipper, a giant spoon that points the way to the North Star.
constellations.find: Look north on a clear night and find the big spoon shape. Follow the two stars at the end of the spoon's bowl upwards and you will reach Polaris, the North Star.

constellations.name: Ursa Minor
constellations.story: The Little Dipper is the Great Bear's baby. Its handle ends with Polaris, the North Star, which sits almost exactly above Earth's North Pole. Because the whole sky spins around it, Polaris looks like it stands still while every other star goes for a ride.
constellations.find: Find the Big Dipper first, then follow the two stars at the end of its bowl upward. The next bright star is Polaris, the tip of the Little Dipper's handle.

constellations.name: Cassiopeia
constellations.story: Cassiopeia was a proud queen who boasted that she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs. The sea god was so cross that he sent a monster to her kingdom. Her stars form a bright letter W, spinning around the North Star all night long as if she can never sit still.
constellations.find: On autumn and winter evenings look north, opposite the Big Dipper. The five bright stars make a clear W or M shape.

constellations.name: Orion
constellations.story: Orion was the greatest hunter in the world, so tall he could wade across the sea. He carries a club and a shield, and three bright stars make his belt. Two of his stars are supergiants: red Betelgeuse, a dying star, and blue-white Rigel, one of the brightest stars we can see.
constellations.find: The easiest constellation of all! In winter look for three stars in a straight line, close together. That is Orion's belt.

constellations.name: Taurus
constellations.story: Taurus the bull is charging across the winter sky. His angry orange eye is Aldebaran, an old giant star. On his shoulder sits a tiny sparkly group called the Pleiades, or the Seven Sisters. Ancient people used this little cluster to test whether someone had good eyesight. How many can you count?
constellations.find: Look for Orion's belt, then follow the line of three stars up and to the right to reach a V shape of stars - that is the bull's face, with Aldebaran glowing orange.

constellations.name: Canis Major
constellations.story: Canis Major is Orion's loyal hunting dog, running at his heels. It holds Sirius, the brightest star in the entire night sky. Sirius is only about nine light years away, which is very close for a star - that is why it shines so bright and steady.
constellations.find: Find Orion's belt and follow the three stars down and to the left. The dazzling star you reach is Sirius, the dog's nose.

constellations.name: Canis Minor
constellations.story: Canis Minor is the smaller of Orion's two hunting dogs. Bright Procyon marks its head. Procyon is Greek for 'before the dog', because it rises just before Sirius in the sky. Procyon, Sirius and Betelgeuse make a huge triangle that people call the Winter Triangle.
constellations.find: Look to the left of Orion's shoulders and you will see one very bright star, Procyon, with a fainter one beside it.

constellations.name: Gemini
constellations.story: Castor and Pollux were twin brothers who shared everything. When Castor died, Pollux begged Zeus to let them stay together, so Zeus placed them both in the sky. Sailors believed the twins brought good luck and calm winds to their ships.
constellations.find: Find Orion's bright shoulder stars, then follow a line up and to the left. You will see two bright stars side by side - the heads of the twins.

constellations.name: Leo
constellations.story: Leo is the Nemean lion, a beast with skin so tough that no arrow could pierce it. The hero Hercules defeated it with his bare hands. Leo's brightest star, Regulus, means 'little king' and sits right on the path the Sun travels across the sky.
constellations.find: Look for a backwards question mark of stars in the spring sky. The dot at the bottom of the question mark is bright Regulus. East of it lies a triangle for the lion's tail.

constellations.name: Cygnus
constellations.story: Cygnus is a swan flying along the Milky Way. Its long neck stretches toward the south and its wings are wide open. In the story, Zeus turned himself into a swan to make friends with a kind queen. Cygnus also holds the Northern Cross, a helpful signpost for summer nights.
constellations.find: In summer and autumn look high overhead for a big cross of stars. The brightest star at the top of the cross is Deneb.

constellations.name: Lyra
constellations.story: Lyra is the harp of Orpheus, whose music was so beautiful that rivers stopped flowing to listen. Vega, its brightest star, is one of the closest bright stars to Earth. In about twelve thousand years, Vega will take its turn as the North Star.
constellations.find: Look for the brightest star high overhead on a summer evening. Vega is a corner of the Summer Triangle and has a little parallelogram of stars hanging beneath it.

constellations.name: Aquila
constellations.story: Aquila is the eagle that carried Zeus's thunderbolts across the sky. Its eye is Altair, a star that spins so fast it is squashed into an oval shape. Altair, Vega and Deneb form the Summer Triangle, a giant shape you can use to find your way around the summer sky.
constellations.find: Find Vega, then look down and to the right for a bright star with a fainter star on each side. That is the eagle flying along the Milky Way.

constellations.name: Scorpius
constellations.story: Scorpius is the scorpion that stung the hunter Orion. The two are never in the sky at the same time - when the scorpion rises, Orion runs away. The scorpion's heart is Antares, a red supergiant so huge that if it replaced our Sun it would swallow Mars.
constellations.find: On summer nights look low in the south for a curvy line of bright stars ending in a hooked tail. The reddish star in the middle is Antares.

constellations.name: Sagittarius
constellations.story: Sagittarius is a centaur - half human, half horse - drawing a bow and arrow. He is aiming at the scorpion's heart. The middle of our own galaxy lies behind Sagittarius, so if you look here with binoculars you will see an enormous crowd of stars.
constellations.find: Look low in the south on summer evenings, below and left of Scorpius. Its main stars make a shape like a teapot with a spout and handle.

constellations.name: Pegasus
constellations.story: Pegasus was a magical horse with wings that flew out of the sea. When it landed on a mountain, a spring of poetry water burst out of the ground. Four of its stars make a huge square called the Great Square of Pegasus, easy to spot on autumn nights.
constellations.find: Look east on autumn evenings for four stars marking a giant square. Enif, the horse's nose, stretches away from the square's corner.

constellations.name: Andromeda
constellations.story: Andromeda was a princess chained to a rock by the sea, waiting for a monster. The hero Perseus flew in on his winged sandals and saved her. If you look just above the middle star of Andromeda you can see the Andromeda Galaxy, the farthest thing your eyes can see without a telescope.
constellations.find: Start at the top left corner of the Great Square of Pegasus - that star also belongs to Andromeda. Two more bright stars lead away from the square.

constellations.name: Perseus
constellations.story: Perseus was the hero who cut off the head of Medusa, whose hair was made of snakes. He is holding it up in the sky. One of his stars, Algol, is called the Demon Star: every two and a half days it gets much dimmer, then bright again, like a slow blink.
constellations.find: Look between Andromeda and the bright V of Cassiopeia on autumn and winter nights. A curving line of stars makes the hero's path.

constellations.name: Auriga
constellations.story: Auriga is a chariot driver holding two baby goats in his arms. The brightest star, Capella, means 'little she-goat'. Capella looks like one star but it is really four stars dancing around each other, and it is the sixth brightest star in the night sky.
constellations.find: Look overhead on winter evenings for a bright star with a little pentagon of fainter stars nearby. Capella is almost straight above you.

constellations.name: Bootes
constellations.story: Bootes is a herdsman who follows the Great Bear around the sky, or perhaps he invented the plough. His star Arcturus is a giant orange sun and the brightest star in the northern half of the sky. Long ago, sailors could find it by following the curve of the Big Dipper's handle: 'arc to Arcturus'.
constellations.find: Find the Big Dipper, follow the curve of its handle until you bump into a big orange star. That is Arcturus. The rest of Bootes makes a kite shape above it.

constellations.name: Virgo
constellations.story: Virgo is a kind maiden holding an ear of wheat. Her bright star Spica is a pair of blue-white stars so close together that they circle each other every four days. Virgo is also home to a giant cluster of galaxies, with more than a thousand islands of stars like our own Milky Way.
constellations.find: Find Arcturus, then follow the same curve onwards: 'arc to Arcturus, speed on to Spica'. Spica is the only really bright star in this part of the sky.

constellations.name: Crux
constellations.story: Crux is the smallest constellation of all, but one of the most famous. It is a cross of bright stars that points the way south, just like the Big Dipper points north. Travelers in the southern hemisphere have used it for navigation for thousands of years. It even appears on several countries' flags.
constellations.find: Only visible from the southern hemisphere or the tropics. Look for a compact kite-shaped cross of four bright stars in the southern Milky Way.

constellations.name: Centaurus
constellations.story: Centaurus is a wise centaur who taught heroes and doctors. His foot is pointed at the Southern Cross. The star Rigil Kentaurus is better known as Alpha Centauri, and it is our closest star neighbour after the Sun - though it is still over four light years away.
constellations.find: From the southern hemisphere, look for two brilliant stars low in the south, to the right of the Southern Cross.

constellations.name: Draco
constellations.story: Draco is a long, twisting dragon that wraps around the Little Dipper. Four thousand years ago its star Thuban was the North Star, and the pyramids of Egypt were lined up with it. Because Earth wobbles like a spinning top, the North Star slowly changes over thousands of years.
constellations.find: Find the Big Dipper, then look for a long line of stars curling between the two dippers and around the Little Dipper's bowl.

constellations.name: Cepheus
constellations.story: Cepheus was the king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. His stars make a simple house shape near the North Star. One of his stars, the Garnet Star, is one of the reddest stars you can see - like a glowing ember.
constellations.find: Look for the house-shaped outline between Cassiopeia and the North Star on autumn and winter evenings.

constellations.name: Hercules
constellations.story: Hercules was the strongest hero of all, famous for his twelve mighty labours. His stars make a big keystone shape. On summer nights you can find a huge faint blur inside him: the Hercules Cluster, a ball of hundreds of thousands of stars.
constellations.find: Look between Vega and Arcturus on summer evenings for a square of four stars - the keystone - with lines of stars stretching out from its corners.

constellations.name: Carina
constellations.story: Carina is the keel of a great ship, the Argo, which carried heroes on a famous voyage. Its star Canopus is the second brightest star in the whole sky, a supergiant shining many thousands of times brighter than our Sun.
constellations.find: From the southern hemisphere, look for a very bright star low in the south. Canopus is so bright that astronauts use it to steer spacecraft.

constellations.name: Ophiuchus
constellations.story: Ophiuchus is a doctor holding a giant snake. Legend says he watched one snake bring another back to life with a herb, and learned the secret of healing. He is the thirteenth constellation of the zodiac - the Sun actually passes through him too, but he is left out of the usual twelve.
constellations.find: Look above Scorpius on summer evenings for a big, lopsided rectangle of stars. The brightest corner is Rasalhague.

constellations.name: Aquarius
constellations.story: Aquarius is a boy pouring water from a jar, and the water flows all the way to a star called Fomalhaut. Ancient people saw this constellation in the rainy season and named it after water. It is a big, faint pattern, best found on autumn evenings.
constellations.find: Look in the south on autumn evenings, below Pegasus, for a faint Y-shaped group of stars.

constellations.name: Libra
constellations.story: Libra is a pair of weighing scales, held by the maiden Virgo. Long ago these stars were actually the scorpion's claws - their names still mean 'northern claw' and 'southern claw'. The Sun is in Libra at the start of autumn, when day and night are the same length.
constellations.find: Find Scorpius and look just to its right for a small quadrilateral of stars in spring.

constellations.name: Crater
constellations.story: Crater is the cup of Apollo, a golden goblet used at feasts. A crow was sent to fetch water in it and fibbed about why it was late, so Apollo threw both cup and crow into the sky. The two constellations sit close together, which is why the crow is always beside the cup.
constellations.find: Look between Leo and Virgo in spring for a faint, slightly bent cup of stars.

constellations.name: Delphinus
constellations.story: Delphinus is the dolphin that convinced a sea nymph to marry the sea god. As a reward it was placed in the sky. Its two brightest stars have unusual names, Rotanev and Sualocin - read backwards they spell 'Nicolaus Venator', an astronomer's clever joke.
constellations.find: Look for a small, pretty kite of stars just left of the Summer Triangle on summer and autumn evenings.

constellations.name: Corvus
constellations.story: Corvus is Apollo's crow, sent to fetch water in Crater. The crow wasted time waiting for a fig to ripen and told a fib about a water snake. Apollo saw through the lie and put the crow in the sky beside the cup it never filled.
constellations.find: Look right of Virgo on spring evenings for four stars shaped like a little sail or kite.

constellations.name: Aries
constellations.story: Aries is the golden ram with a magical fleece. Two children escaped on its back, but the ram lost its golden coat on the way. Long ago, Aries contained the point where the Sun crossed into the sky's northern half each spring, so it is called the first constellation of the zodiac.
constellations.find: Look for a crooked line of three stars, with Hamal the brightest, between Pegasus and the Pleiades on autumn evenings.
